name: Quality Systems for AI Devices
blurb: How device quality management changes for AI.
title: Quality Systems for AI Devices
answer: AI devices run on the same quality system as other devices, now aligned with ISO 13485 in the United States since the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation took effect on 2 February 2026. AI adds data management, model training records and change control for retraining to that system.

reading.body:
AI devices do not get a separate quality system. Since 2 February 2026 the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation aligns US device requirements with ISO 13485, and AI devices run inside that same system.

What AI adds is data and models as controlled design elements. Training, validation and test datasets are design inputs, so their sources, labelling and quality need records, and their provenance and changes need document control. Model versions, training runs and evaluation results need traceable records. Retraining is a change, so it goes through design and change control, with post-market performance feeding back into risk management and corrective action.

The practical shift for a medtech team is treating training data like a specification rather than a side artefact. That is a documentation and process burden, not a compute or power one, and the data here says nothing about how large those datasets are, how often models are retrained, or what any of it costs. It also covers the US alignment only. The related EU AI Act material is referenced but not described, so the European position for these devices is not established by this data.

explainer:
A quality management system is the set of procedures a device maker uses to control design, production, changes, complaints and corrective actions. In the United States the Quality Management System Regulation, effective February 2026, aligns FDA requirements with the international standard ISO 13485, so one system can serve both markets.

For AI devices the system needs extensions. Training, validation and test data must be controlled as design inputs, with records of their sources, labelling and quality. Model versions, training runs and evaluation results need traceable records. Changes to data or models go through design and change control, and post-market performance monitoring feeds back into risk management and corrective action. Treating data and models as controlled elements of the design, not as side artefacts, is the core shift.

What a quality management system is for

Every medical device manufacturer must run a quality management system: documented processes for design, risk management, supplier control, production, complaint handling and corrective action, audited by regulators and notified bodies. The international standard most regulators recognise is ISO 13485, and the FDA has aligned its own quality regulation to it. The system exists so that a device is designed, built and maintained the same controlled way every time.

What AI adds to the system

An AI device has components a conventional device does not: training data, a model, and a process for updating it. The quality system has to cover them. Design controls extend to data requirements, data provenance and model development records. Risk management considers failure modes such as drift, bias and performance on unseen inputs. Supplier controls cover the data sources, cloud services and model components bought from others. Post market processes add performance monitoring. And change control defines when a model update is a minor change and when it needs a new review, ideally agreed with the regulator in advance.

Standards catching up

Standards bodies are writing AI specific guidance to sit alongside ISO 13485, and the FDA and international regulators have published good machine learning practice principles that map onto quality system elements. Manufacturers do not wait for the final standards. They document how their existing system addresses each AI specific element, because that is the question an auditor will ask, and a clear mapping answers it.
